title: The Pig That Everybody Underestimates

blocks.prompt: The Nose That Does Everything
blocks.text: A pig sees the world with its nose. The round snout on the front of its face is tough and strong. A pig uses it like a shovel. It pushes the snout into the ground and digs and digs. This is called rooting. Under the dirt, the pig finds roots and nuts and bugs to eat. A pig's nose is very good at smelling. It can smell food buried deep down, food it cannot see at all. A pig's eyes are not very good. But a pig hardly ever gets lost. It just follows its nose.

3.title: The Pig That Everybody Underestimates
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then answer the questions.

notes: Pigs have almost no working sweat glands
Mud cools better than sweat does
Pale pig skin can sunburn
Mud pulls ticks and flies off the skin
Pigs keep their toilet far from their bed

blocks.prompt: Why a Pig Rolls in Mud
blocks.text:
People say pigs are dirty. Pigs are not dirty. Pigs are smart about staying cool.

Here is the problem. You have sweat glands all over your skin. When you get hot, you sweat, the sweat dries off your skin, and that cools you down. A pig cannot do this. A pig has almost no working sweat glands. On a hot day, a pig has no way to cool itself from the inside.

So the pig goes to the mud. It lies down and rolls until it is coated all over. Then it stands up. The water in the mud dries off the pig slowly, and as it dries, it pulls the heat away. A coat of mud works better than sweat, and it lasts much longer.

The mud does two other jobs. Pigs have pale skin, and pale skin burns in the sun, so the mud works like sunscreen. Mud also traps ticks and biting flies. When the pig scratches the dried mud off against a tree, the bugs come off with it.

One more thing. Given enough room, a pig picks one corner to use as a toilet and keeps it far away from where it eats and sleeps. A pig in the mud is not being dirty. It is putting on its coat.

answers: sweat dries off your skin and takes the heat with it
a pig has almost no working sweat glands

4.title: The Pig That Everybody Underestimates
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Piglets learn their names in about two weeks
Pigs use mirrors to find hidden food
Four pigs learned a joystick video game in 2021
Pigs have around 15,000 taste buds
Pigs make more than 20 different sounds

blocks.prompt: The Pig That Played a Video Game
blocks.text:
Ask someone to name a clever animal and they will say a dolphin, or a chimpanzee, or a dog. Almost nobody says a pig. That is a mistake.

Start with something easy. A piglet learns its own name in about two weeks and will come when you call it. Now try something harder. Put a pig in a pen with a mirror, angled so the mirror shows a bowl of food tucked behind a barrier where the pig cannot see it directly. Most animals charge at the mirror and hunt around behind it. Pigs try that once, then stop, turn around, and walk straight to the real bowl. They have worked out something difficult: a reflection is not a thing. It is information about a place.

Then there is the joystick. In 2021, researchers at Purdue University gave four pigs a computer screen, a joystick, and a target to hit. Move the cursor into the target, get a treat. The pigs had never held anything in their lives, so they shoved the joystick around with their snouts. They were slow. They were clumsy. And they hit the target far more often than random guessing can explain, which means they understood that the thing under their nose was moving the thing on the screen.

A pig has no hands, poor eyesight, and a body built for digging up roots. It solved a puzzle designed by people, using a tool made for human hands, anyway. We keep inventing tests to measure how much other animals are like us. The pig keeps passing tests it has no business passing.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in full sentences.

answers: (a mirror shows food they cannot see directly; they learn the reflection tells them where the real food is)
(inference: it shows the joystick was much harder for a pig than for us, so their success counts for more)
(random luck would give a low score, so a high score means they understood the joystick moved the cursor)
(opinion: the mud, the smell, the fact that we farm them)

5.title: The Pig That Everybody Underestimates
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Domestic pigs descend from wild boar, Sus scrofa
Domesticated at least twice, about 9,000 years ago
Once in the Near East, once in China
Ancient bone DNA shows two separate starts
Feral pigs live wild in dozens of US states

blocks.prompt: The Boar in the Barnyard
blocks.text:
Nine thousand years ago there were no pigs. There were wild boar: dark, bristled, quick-tempered animals with tusks, ranging through the forests of Europe and Asia. Then people began keeping them, and the keeping changed them.

It happened at least twice, independently, in places with no contact with each other. Farmers in what is now Turkey were penning boar at roughly the same time that farmers in China were penning their own. We know this because DNA pulled from ancient bones shows two separate beginnings, not one clever idea spreading along a trade route.

What people did next was slow and mostly accidental. Nobody sat down and designed a pig. The boar that stayed calm around humans got fed and got to breed. The ones that panicked or charged did not last long enough to raise piglets. Generation after generation, the calm bred with the calm, and the bodies followed the temperament. Tusks shrank. Legs shortened. The heavy fighting shoulders of a forest animal softened into the round body of an animal that eats and grows. Many pigs turned pink, because a dark bristled coat hides a boar in a forest and hides nothing at all in a pen. Once a trait stops earning its keep, it tends to drift away.

Here is the part worth sitting with. Domestication is not permanent, and it is not deep. Let farm pigs loose in the woods and their descendants come back. Within a few generations they grow thick coarse bristles, heavy shoulders, and long tusks. The United States now has millions of feral pigs doing precisely this across dozens of states, tearing up crops, wrecking stream banks, and outrunning almost everyone sent to catch them. They are not a new species. They are not even a different animal. They are the same pig, with the barn taken away.

Nine thousand years of breeding sounds like a long time. It turns out the boar was never far under the surface. It was just waiting to be needed again.

6.title: The Pig That Everybody Underestimates
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Pig heart valves have been used in people for over 50 years
Insulin came from pig pancreases before 1982
January 2022: first gene-edited pig heart transplant
That donor pig had 10 genetic edits
Pigs reach human organ size in about 6 months
Pigs learn names, use mirrors, and solved a joystick game

blocks.prompt: A Pig's Heart
blocks.text:
In January 2022, surgeons in Baltimore opened the chest of a dying man named David Bennett and gave him the heart of a pig. The heart beat. Bennett lived another two months. Most of the coverage treated the operation as a story about the future of medicine. It is also a story about how strange our relationship with this animal has become.

The pig was never the obvious donor. Chimpanzees and baboons sit far closer to us on the family tree, and for a while surgeons tried them. But primates breed slowly, are difficult and expensive to raise, and are the wrong size: a baboon heart cannot move enough blood to keep an adult human alive. A pig can. Pigs grow fast, breed well, reach roughly human organ size in about six months, and their bodies are plumbed on something close to our scale.

Medicine noticed this a long time ago. Before 1982, people with diabetes injected insulin harvested from the pancreases of pigs and cattle. Heart valves cut from pigs have been sewn into human patients for over fifty years. Surgeons still dress severe burns with pig skin. The pig has been quietly holding parts of us together for decades, and almost nobody thinks about it.

What stopped whole organs was the immune system. Pig cells carry a sugar that human blood identifies instantly as foreign, and the rejection that follows is fast and total. Bennett's donor was not an ordinary pig. Its genome had been edited in ten places: some genes switched off so the offending sugar was never built, some human genes added to keep the immune response calm, others adjusted so the heart would not outgrow the chest it was going into. The animal was designed, from conception, to be spare parts for a person.

Here is where it gets uncomfortable. The same decades of research that proved how useful pigs are also proved how much is happening inside them. Pigs learn their own names within weeks and come when called. They use mirrors to locate food they cannot see directly, which means they grasp that a reflection carries information about a place rather than being a place. In 2021, researchers at Purdue University taught four pigs to play a simple video game, steering a cursor into a target with a joystick they pushed around with their snouts. The pigs scored well above chance. Nothing about a pig was built for a joystick, and they did it anyway.

So we have an animal clever enough to solve a puzzle we invented, using a tool we designed for hands it does not have, and we are editing its genes so that we can take its heart out. Both things are true at once. The same patient curiosity produced both results, and neither cancels the other.

Nobody is required to feel good about this. But the choice is not really between using pigs and leaving them alone. Bennett was dying. The kidney waiting lists are long and people die on them. Meanwhile, most of us eat pigs without a second thought, which is a far larger use of them and asks far less of us. The question is not whether a pig's life should count for something. It is why we only seem to ask when a heart is on the table.
